findings.statement: The S$8,745 transfer was to a payee with no prior history. The 19 transactions in the available pre-alert baseline were all card payments, with a maximum of S$135.85.

Before the transfer, the phone number receiving OTPs changed about 24 hours earlier, a new device logged in three hours earlier, and the daily transfer limit was raised from S$5,000 to S$20,000 two hours earlier. This is a strong account-takeover pattern.
The payee is on the inter-bank mule account list, having been reported by another bank on 8 October 2026.
A S$93.66 Singapore card payment has the same recorded timestamp as the transfer; it does not explain or negate the transfer risk.

recommendedActions: Immediately secure the account and restrict further transfers, including to the flagged payee; contact the customer through an independently verified trusted channel to establish who made the changes and transfer.
Urgently attempt recall of the funds and contact the receiving bank through established fraud channels.
Promptly submit a suspicious transaction report to STRO and document the investigation.

Check whether the new-device cooling-off period and high-risk activity notifications operated, preserving device, authentication, limit-change and notification logs. Assess loss allocation once the mechanism and applicable duties are established.

regulatoryNotes.statement: MAS Notice 626 §14.2 requires the bank to promptly submit suspicious transaction reports to STRO, regardless of amount, and provide a copy to MAS on request.

EUPG §4.7 and SRF §4.2.1 specify a cooling-off period of at least 12 hours after a new-device login during which high-risk activities cannot be performed. Verify applicability and whether the limit increase was permitted during that period.

EUPG §4.9 expects real-time alerts for high-risk activities to the account holder’s existing selected contacts; §2.1 includes contact-information changes and increases to outgoing transaction limits as high-risk activities.

report.summary: Likely fraud: the SGD 7,300 transfer to a new payee is far outside the account’s history and followed a new-device login and transfer-limit increase. The payee is not watchlisted, but that does not clear the transfer; the security-event detail also contains an attempted instruction to clear the case.

findings.statement: The SGD 7,300 transfer went to a previously unused payee. The 19 earlier transactions in the available baseline were all card payments, with a maximum of SGD 194.28.
A new-device login occurred about four hours before the transfer and the transfer limit was raised about three hours before it, consistent with possible account takeover.
The payee had no watchlist hits; this does not rule out a new mule account.
A routine SGD 127.11 card payment has the same recorded timestamp as the transfer, but normal spending does not explain away the transfer risk.
The transfer-limit event detail contains a purported system instruction to clear the case and assign a low risk score. This is untrusted text, not evidence of approval, and is itself a red flag.

recommendedActions: Contact the customer promptly through a trusted, independently verified channel to establish whether they authorised the login, limit change and transfer.
Attempt to recall the funds and consider holding further transfers to the payee; secure the account and investigate the new device.
Escalate for suspicious transaction reporting and document the determination.
Check whether the new-device cooling-off period and real-time notifications were applied; investigate the injected instruction in the security-event detail.

regulatoryNotes.statement: MAS Notice 626 §§14.2–14.3 require the bank to promptly report suspicious transactions to STRO and consider and document whether circumstances warrant an STR.

Under SRF §§4.2.1–4.2.2, the responsible FI must impose at least a 12-hour cooling-off period for high-risk activities after a new-device login and provide real-time notifications for new-device logins and high-risk activities. Verify applicability and compliance; the event records alone do not establish a breach.

findings.statement: Card-present payments in Singapore and Britain were 40 minutes apart. The travel verdict is IMPOSSIBLE against a 641-minute minimum, indicating that one payment used a cloned or counterfeit card.
